Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-07

Duration: ~49 minutes
Attendees: Alex Monroe (Redwood AE); Sana Kapoor (Redwood SE); Diego Fernandez (Redwood SE); Priya Rao (NovaEdge CTO); Tom Gregson (NovaEdge SRE); Maya Chen (NovaEdge ML Eng)

Summary (auto-gen):
Quick POC sync — looked at this week's latency snapshots, some TTFT gains after we flipped priority routing + light hedging. Streaming path still shows microburst at ~400-600ms occasionally for short sequences. Discussed kernel pick tradeoffs for mixed seqlen traffic and next steps to validate in a larger sample.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we'll get started. Quick roll call, and then Sana will walk through the perf snapshots.
[00:12] Priya: Hi, Priya here. Thanks.
[00:15] Tom: Tom — good morning.
[00:18] Maya: Maya on my side.
[00:22] Alex: Great. Sana, over to you.
[00:25] Sana: Cool thanks. I'll share my screen, bear with me, um, so this week's key thing was we enabled per-route priority routing with a small hedging window — basically 10ms hedge to the faster kernel for short seq lens. We also left large sequences on the throughput kernel. The headline: median TTFT down about 22%, P95 down around 12% on streaming workloads we ran in the staging cluster.
[01:05] Priya: Ok that's promising. When you say "hedging" — can you explain the exact flow? We had some confusion earlier where hedging sometimes doubled GPU usage.
[01:14] Sana: Yeah totally. So hedging here is conservative — we send a parallel probe to the lower-latency kernel if the request is not flowing through the fast path in X ms, X configured as 10. The probe is cheap because for streaming we only probe the first chunk. If the probe wins we continue on that kernel, otherwise we cancel. It's not full duplicate generation which is why GPU cost didn't spike in our runs.
[01:38] Tom: I heard "probe" — is that a duplicate token? I'm worried about billing too — does this count double?
[01:45] Diego: Good question. On the Redwood side the probe is accounted as a lightweight probe token; you will see a small token bump in the logs but nothing like a full duplicate. We instrumented it in the metrics, and the token delta was ~1.2% for our mixed workload.
[02:03] Maya: The streaming microbursts — can you call out what sequence lengths triggered the spikes? We saw them at 8-20 tokens but not consistent.
[02:12] Sana: Yes — in our sampling the microbursts were most frequent on very short sequences where the runtime switches kernels mid-stream because of an aggressive batcher. Basically batcher tight windows + 1-2 token sequences cause jitter.
[02:28] Alex: Right, that's the seq-len corridor problem we've chatted about. We can mitigate by either special-casing very short sequences to always go to the fast low-latency kernel, or by tweaking the batcher to hold an extra X ms before packing. Both have tradeoffs.
[02:41] Priya: If we special-case shorts to fast kernel, what happens to throughput cost?
[02:47] Sana: There's a small throughput tax if you move too many requests to the fast kernel. Our recommendation was thresholding — e.g., sequences <= 6 tokens — route straight to fast kernel, everything else evaluated with seqlen histogram and cost sensitivity. For NovaEdge's histogram (which you shared last week partially) that looked like ~14% of traffic. So cost increases about ~6% in our sim.
[03:10] Tom: That might be acceptable given our latency goals, but I need exact numbers. Can you share the raw sim?
[03:15] Alex: Yep we'll post the spreadsheet with the model.
[03:19] Maya: Another question — prefix or KV cache: is that safe for our doc prompts? Some of our payloads have PII, and we need to be sure cache eviction and encryption are tight.
[03:31] Diego: Cache is optional. For hosted POC we used prefix caching with customer-aware isolation — it's encrypted at rest, and we can hook into KMS. I will note our logs showed no leakage across tenants in the sim. For Private/VPC we can enable customer-managed KMS/HSM.
[03:49] Priya: Good. We will still need SOC2 documentation on cache lifecycles.
[03:54] Alex: We'll attach the security packet after the call.
[03:58] Priya: Thanks.
[04:01] Alex: Back to the perf — Sana, can you show the kernel-selection deltas?
[04:05] Sana: Sure. On our staging set we toggled between three kernels: fast-lat (opt-attn), throughput (wide-batch), and a quantized fallback. The fast-lat kernel gave us the best median TTFT on short seqs; throughput kernel dominated for seqlens > 256. The quantized fallback saved ~30% cost but added latency variance, particularly in microburst scenarios because of quant decode overhead.
[04:40] Maya: That matches what we saw in-house with the quantized clone. We saw worse tail behavior. Is there a way to keep quant for large batches only?
[04:50] Sana: Yes you can tier quantized models to high-throughput pools only; Redwood's routing policy can prefer quant for throughput pool and avoid it for low-latency paths. That said, if you have a lot of mixed traffic, the routing layer has to be strict about which requests are eligible.
[05:06] Tom: What about function calling / tool calls — do they force us into the slower path? We use a lot of tool loads.
[05:12] Diego: Tool calls that require longer context will naturally push seq len up. But for first-token lat we can still favor the fast kernel by trimming tool context for the initial token if tolerable. There are product flags for partial-tool-context.
[05:25] Priya: Hmm, need to be careful there.
[05:28] Alex: We'll note that as an opt-in config for the pilot.
[05:32] [06:00] Sana: Quick note on metrics: we are reporting TTFT as first-byte seen by client; Redwood's observability differentiates runtime-ttft vs network-ttft. In NovaEdge's staging there was ~8ms of network overhead on average — that won't go away unless we move region.
[06:21] Tom: We're in us-west-2, yes. Can we route through a nearer region? Not really; our infra is us-west-2 only for compliance.
[06:29] Alex: Ok, so we'll include network delta when we produce final numbers.
[06:33] Maya: Another oddity — on last week's run some streaming sessions terminated early due to client cancelation, which threw off averages. We need per-session sampling.
[06:43] Diego: Agreed. We'll provide session-level logs so you can filter cancels.
[06:47] Priya: On security: Tom flagged that our legal needs VPC peering diagrams and audit log retention guarantees.
[06:55] Alex: We'll attach a compact VPC note and the SOC2 and audit log policy.
[06:58] Tom: Thanks.
[07:01] Maya: For the 1k-sample run, are you planning to run on Redwood Hosted or Dedicated? That will change kernel choices.
[07:09] Sana: Good call — we'll run both. First run on Hosted to get a baseline, second on Dedicated-like pool (we'll emulate) to show differences. That will give you realistic delta for Dedicated purchase decisions.
[07:22] Priya: Can the Dedicated emulate our single-tenant KMS behavior?
[07:26] Diego: For the emulation we can turn on sample per-tenant keys in the staging environment; real customer-managed KMS is only in Private, but we can approximate the crypto path for latency impact.
[07:38] Tom: Ok. Also curious — you mentioned hedging window of 10ms; can we make that adaptive? Some of our traffic is bursty.
[07:45] Sana: We can. There are adaptive hedging policies that look at recent RTT distribution and widen/narrow hedging. We recommended starting fixed-10ms for stability then move to adaptive if you want.
[07:58] Maya: That may reduce unnecessary probes.
[08:01] Alex: Alright let's talk risks and success criteria. Priya, what's your threshold?
[08:07] Priya: Ideally TTFT median < 120ms and P95 < 350ms for streaming API. If we can get within 10% of that, we'll consider the pilot successful enough to move to the next phase. Cost uplift should be under 15% vs our baseline.
[08:24] Alex: Good — we'll target that.
[08:27] Sana: Quick item: earlier we saw some mis-labelled metric name in your account — the route was called "nova-tst" which made our routing rules mismatch. We patched it but please standardize route naming; we'll send naming conventions.
[08:40] Tom: Yep we'll align.
[08:42] Alex: Cool. Any final questions?
[08:45] Maya: One last — can you include a sample traffic replay command so we can run locally?
[08:48] Diego: Yep I'll paste the curl/wrangler script in the notes.
[08:52] Priya: Perfect.
[08:54] Alex: Ok let's recap next steps — we'll run the 1k mixed workload, post the spreadsheet, Sana will prepare kernel deep-dive, and NovaEdge will upload sample prompts and histogram. Any other items?
[09:06] Priya: No, that's it. Thanks.
[09:09] Alex: Thanks all — we'll follow up in calendar.
